<div class="project-content">

<p class="lede-para">
  A Kaggle-style regression problem: predict <code>log_total</code> — total customer spend on a log scale — from
  demographic and transaction features. The interesting part was not the winning model but how narrow the gap between
  models turned out to be, and how much of the improvement came from feature work instead.
</p>

<div class="results">
  <div class="result"><span class="num">0.113</span><span class="lbl">RMSE (random forest)</span></div>
  <div class="result"><span class="num">0.003</span><span class="lbl">Standard error</span></div>
  <div class="result"><span class="num">&gt;0.95</span><span class="lbl">R² on held-out data</span></div>
  <div class="result"><span class="num">5</span><span class="lbl">Model families compared</span></div>
</div>

<h2>Preprocessing</h2>

<ul>
  <li>Handled missing values, then normalized and transformed the skewed spending variables — the log transform on the
  response is what makes the residuals behave.</li>
  <li>Screened features on correlation and importance before modeling rather than throwing everything at the wall.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Model selection</h2>

<ul>
  <li>Compared <strong>linear regression, ridge, lasso, random forest and KNN regression</strong> under the same
  cross-validated protocol.</li>
  <li>Tuned hyperparameters with cross-validation in <strong>caret</strong>, so the comparison was between tuned models
  rather than default settings.</li>
  <li><strong>KNN underperformed</strong> the tree-based models — unsurprising given the mix of categorical and
  count features, where distance metrics get awkward.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Feature engineering</h2>

<ul>
  <li>Found <code>count_hh4</code> and <code>count_G</code> — household size and order-count features — to be the
  strongest correlates of <code>log_total</code>.</li>
  <li>Tested interactions between income level and purchase frequency, which sharpened the fit for high-frequency
  households.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Result</h2>

<ul>
  <li>The final <strong>random forest</strong> reached <strong>RMSE 0.1129</strong> (SE 0.0030) with R² above 0.9587.</li>
  <li><strong>Household size, order count, and income level</strong> were the significant predictors of Amazon spend —
  the model is essentially learning that more people in a household with more orders spend more, and quantifying by
  how much.</li>
  <li>Worth naming the limitation: the strong R² partly reflects predictors that are close relatives of the response.
  It's a good predictive model and a weak causal one.</li>
</ul>
